      "title": "Device limit can be bypassed by omitting the client-supplied device header",
      "body": "TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty, and Anonymous.Authenticate only rejects authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Because the device ID header is supplied by the client, an anonymous client can omit it and avoid being counted or blocked, while normal UI clients that send the header are limited. The configured device_limit therefore cannot reliably cap anonymous devices."

      "line": 87,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "Local cache is populated before persistence, allowing blocked devices to bypass the limit on retry",
      "body": "tagDeviceUI stores the device key in the local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, or any other database error, the cache entry is not removed. For the cache TTL, subsequent requests with the same device ID hit the cache and TagDevice returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. A device that was initially rejected by the device limit can therefore retry and bypass the limit, and database failures are also hidden."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go",
      "line": 110,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "concurrency",
      "title": "Device-limit check is not atomic with the insert/update",
      "body": "CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running SELECT COUNT(*) and then, in a separate step, inserting or updating the device. There is no transaction, lock, or conditional database operation tying the count check to the write. Concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can all observe count below device_limit and then all insert new rows, causing the number of active anonymous devices to exceed the configured limit."
    },

      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go",
      "line": 45,
      "severity": "medium",

      "title": "Unauthenticated clients can exhaust the device limit and deny access to new devices",
      "body": "Device IDs come from the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header. When device_limit is enabled, an attacker can send many requests with unique device IDs to fill the active anon_device count. Once the limit is reached, Anonymous.Authenticate rejects unknown devices, so legitimate new anonymous devices can be denied access. This makes the limit exploitable as a denial-of-service vector."
    },

      "file": "pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go",
      "line": 44,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous authentication path",
      "body": "TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine into Anonymous.Authenticate. When device_limit is non-zero, each uncached device triggers a COUNT query plus a database write before the anonymous identity is returned. This adds latency to anonymous requests and can become a performance hotspot on instances with many anonymous devices."

findings.title: Device limit can be bypassed by omitting the client-supplied device header
findings.body: TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty, and Anonymous.Authenticate only rejects authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Because the device ID header is supplied by the client, an anonymous client can omit it and avoid being counted or blocked, while normal UI clients that send the header are limited. The configured device_limit therefore cannot reliably cap anonymous devices.

findings.title: Local cache is populated before persistence, allowing blocked devices to bypass the limit on retry
findings.body: tagDeviceUI stores the device key in the local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, or any other database error, the cache entry is not removed. For the cache TTL, subsequent requests with the same device ID hit the cache and TagDevice returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. A device that was initially rejected by the device limit can therefore retry and bypass the limit, and database failures are also hidden.

findings.title: Device-limit check is not atomic with the insert/update
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running SELECT COUNT(*) and then, in a separate step, inserting or updating the device. There is no transaction, lock, or conditional database operation tying the count check to the write. Concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can all observe count below device_limit and then all insert new rows, causing the number of active anonymous devices to exceed the configured limit.

findings.title: Unauthenticated clients can exhaust the device limit and deny access to new devices
findings.body: Device IDs come from the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header. When device_limit is enabled, an attacker can send many requests with unique device IDs to fill the active anon_device count. Once the limit is reached, Anonymous.Authenticate rejects unknown devices, so legitimate new anonymous devices can be denied access. This makes the limit exploitable as a denial-of-service vector.

findings.title: Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous authentication path
findings.body: TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine into Anonymous.Authenticate. When device_limit is non-zero, each uncached device triggers a COUNT query plus a database write before the anonymous identity is returned. This adds latency to anonymous requests and can become a performance hotspot on instances with many anonymous devices.

findings.title: Missing test that existing devices can still update when the limit is reached
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, unknown device is rejected when the limit is 1. It does not verify that an existing active device can still be updated after the limit is reached. Since returning anonymous devices should remain authenticated, a regression in updateDevice could lock out existing devices without being caught.

findings.title: untagDevice logs the wrong error variable
findings.body: In untagDevice, when DeleteDevice fails the log statement uses the incoming err variable instead of errD, the error returned by DeleteDevice. As a result, the logged error is unrelated to the actual delete failure.
